note: The words people use around you before anyone explains them. Read in order the first time.

groups.title: The machines
groups.blurb: Before anything else: what is actually sitting somewhere, doing the work.

items.one: A machine that follows instructions very fast and never gets bored.
items.like: A cook who only knows how to follow a recipe exactly, but can do it a million times a second without complaining.
items.long: It has a brain that does the thinking (the CPU), a desk to keep the things it is working on right now (memory, or RAM), and a cupboard to keep things for later (the disk). Turn it off and the desk is wiped clean. The cupboard keeps its contents.
items.why: Everything else on this page is just computers talking to each other.

items.one: A computer that stays switched on and waits for people to ask it things.
items.like: A shop that never closes. Somebody is always at the counter, waiting for a customer to walk in.
items.long: It is not a special kind of machine. It is an ordinary computer given a job: sit there, listen, and answer. Your laptop could be a server. It just would not be a very reliable one, because you close the lid and take it home.
items.why: When people say 'the website is on a server', they mean there is a computer somewhere that is awake right now, holding your website.

items.one: A building full of thousands of servers, with very good air conditioning.
items.like: A warehouse where instead of boxes on the shelves, there are computers on the shelves, all humming.
items.long: They are enormous, windowless, cold, and noisy. They have their own power supply, backup generators and armed guards. Amazon owns many of them. When you rent a server from AWS, it is a slice of a machine in one of these buildings.
items.why: The cloud is not in the sky. It is in a building, in a specific country, with a postcode.

items.one: The brain, the desk, and the cupboard.
items.like: A cook: how fast they chop (CPU), how much bench space they have (RAM), and how big the pantry is (disk).
items.long: CPU is measured in cores, or vCPUs. More cores means more things at once. RAM is measured in GB and is fast but forgets everything when the power goes. Disk is also GB, is much slower, and remembers. Run out of RAM and the machine crawls or crashes. Run out of disk and it stops writing.
items.why: Every server you rent is priced on these three numbers. 't3.small, 2 vCPU, 2 GB' is exactly this.

groups.title: How one computer finds another
groups.blurb: The internet is just machines finding each other and passing notes.

items.one: Cables between buildings, letting computers pass messages to each other.
items.like: The road network. Not one road, millions of them, all joined up, owned by different people.
items.long: Most of it is physical cable, including very thick cables lying on the floor of the ocean. Your wifi is only the last few metres. Nothing about it is wireless once it leaves your house.
items.why: When a page loads slowly from another country, it is often because the message really did have to cross an ocean.

items.one: The house number of a computer on the internet.
items.like: A postal address. 142.250.183.14 is a real place, the same way '14 Main Street' is.
items.long: It looks like 142.250.183.14, four numbers with dots. That is IPv4, and the world ran out of them, so there is now IPv6, which is longer and has colons. Every device on the internet has one. Yours changes when your internet provider feels like it.
items.why: Computers only understand addresses. They do not understand names like google.com at all.

items.one: The friendly name of a website, because nobody remembers numbers.
items.like: A shop's name. You say 'the bakery on Main Street', not 'building number 142250183'.
items.long: google.com, kwickprep.com, your-idea.in. You rent it, usually for a year at a time, from a registrar. You never own it outright. Stop paying and somebody else can take it.
items.why: Nobody would use the internet if you had to remember numbers.

items.one: The phone book that turns a name into a number.
items.like: The contacts app on your phone. You tap 'Mum', the phone looks up the real number, and dials it. You never see the number.
items.long: DNS stands for Domain Name System. When you type a name, your computer asks a DNS server 'what is the address for this name?' and gets back an IP address. The answer gets remembered for a while, which is why a change can take hours to reach everybody.
items.why: This is the single most common cause of 'it works for me but not for you'. One person's phone book has been updated and the other's has not.

items.one: One line in that phone book.
items.like: One contact card. A name on the left, a number on the right.
items.long: An A record points a name at an IPv4 address. AAAA points at IPv6. CNAME points one name at another name. MX says where email should go. TXT holds notes, often used to prove you own the domain. TTL is how long everyone is allowed to remember the answer before asking again.
items.why: When somebody says 'point the DNS at the new server', they mean edit one of these lines.

items.one: The door number on a building that has many doors.
items.like: An office block at one address with many doors: reception, deliveries, the fire exit. Same address, different doors for different purposes.
items.long: A server has one address but thousands of numbered doors. Web traffic uses door 80 for plain and 443 for secure. Email uses 25 and 587. Databases use their own, like 5432 or 3306. Closed doors ignore you.
items.why: 'Open port 443' means allow secure web traffic in. Opening the wrong door is how servers get broken into.

items.one: Paying somebody to keep your website on their always-on computer.
items.like: Renting a shop unit in a mall instead of building your own shop.
items.long: You could host a website from a computer in your bedroom. People do. It works until the power cuts, the internet drops, or someone attacks it. Hosting companies handle the power, the cooling, the connection and the security, and charge you monthly.
items.why: AWS is hosting, taken to an extreme: rent by the hour, rent a hundred, give them back at 4pm.

groups.title: What actually happens when you type a website
groups.blurb: Everything above, in order, in about half a second. This is the whole internet in eight steps.

items.term: You type kwickprep.com and press enter
items.one: Eight things happen before you see anything.
items.like: Posting a letter and getting a reply, except it all happens faster than you can blink.
items.long: 1. Your browser checks if it already knows the address. Often it does, and skips ahead. 2. If not, it asks DNS: what is the number for this name? 3. DNS answers with an IP address. 4. Your computer opens a connection to that address, on door 443. 5. The two sides swap certificates and agree a secret code, so nobody in between can read what follows. 6. Your browser sends a short request: please give me the home page. 7. The server sends back HTML, which is the text and the structure, then the browser asks for the images, the styling and the scripts separately. 8. The browser draws it all on your screen. If anything in that chain is slow, the page is slow.
items.why: Every AWS service you will meet sits at one of these eight steps. Route 53 is step 2. CloudFront is step 7. EC2 is the server in step 6.

groups.title: Talking, and talking safely
groups.blurb: The language computers use, and the envelope they put it in.

items.one: The language browsers and servers use to ask for things.
items.like: A very polite, very limited conversation. 'Please give me this.' 'Here it is.' That is nearly all of it.
items.long: GET means give me something. POST means here is something, do something with it. The reply comes with a number: 200 means fine, 404 means I do not have that, 500 means I broke, 403 means you are not allowed.
items.why: When somebody says 'we are getting 500s', they mean the server is falling over.

items.one: The same conversation, sealed in an envelope nobody else can open.
items.like: A postcard versus a sealed letter. On a postcard, every postman can read it.
items.long: The S is for secure. TLS is the technique, SSL is its old name that people still use. It does two things: it scrambles the conversation, and it proves the server really is who it claims to be. The padlock in the browser means both worked.
items.why: Without it, anyone on the same wifi can read the passwords people type into your site.

items.one: The server's ID card, signed by someone the browser trusts.
items.like: A passport. It is only worth anything because a trusted authority issued it and it has not expired.
items.long: It proves this server is genuinely kwickprep.com and not an imposter. Certificates expire, usually every 90 days now. If one expires, every visitor gets a full page scary warning and most turn back.
items.why: An expired certificate takes a site down as surely as a crashed server, and it is entirely avoidable.

items.one: A way for one program to ask another program to do something.
items.like: A waiter. You do not walk into the kitchen. You tell the waiter, and food arrives.
items.long: It is a fixed list of things you may ask for and the exact way to ask. The other program does not show you how it works inside, only what it will accept and what it will send back.
items.why: Your phone app does not talk to the database. It talks to an API, which decides what it is allowed to see.

groups.title: Keeping things and finding them again

items.one: An extremely organised notebook a computer can search instantly.
items.like: A filing cabinet where everything has a label, a place, and rules about what may go where.
items.long: A table is like a spreadsheet: columns for the kind of information, one row per thing. A query is a question you ask it. It can find one row out of ten million in a fraction of a second, because it keeps an index, like the index at the back of a book.
items.why: Almost every app is a nice-looking front door on top of a database.

items.one: Two ways of arranging that notebook.
items.like: A ruled ledger with fixed columns, versus a box of index cards where each card can be different.
items.long: SQL databases have a fixed shape and can answer questions you did not plan for. NoSQL is faster and handles enormous size, but you must know in advance how you will look things up. Ask it a question it was not designed for and it either crawls or refuses.
items.why: This choice is hard to undo later, which is why people argue about it so much.

items.one: Three different ways to keep files, and they are not interchangeable.
items.like: A cupboard you can only reach from one desk, a shared store room, and a vast warehouse you send parcels to.
items.long: A disk (EBS) attaches to one server, like the drive inside a laptop. A shared file system (EFS) can be used by many servers at once. Object storage (S3) is a warehouse: you hand over a whole file and get a link back. You cannot edit a bit in the middle of an S3 file, you replace the whole thing.
items.why: Choosing the wrong one means rewriting your app later. This is a very common early mistake.

items.one: A second copy kept somewhere else, from an earlier moment in time.
items.like: Photocopying your passport and leaving it at your mother's house.
items.long: Copying live data somewhere else is not a backup. If somebody deletes a table, the deletion copies across instantly. A backup is from before the mistake. And a backup nobody has ever restored is not a backup, it is a hope.
items.why: The day you need this is the day you find out whether you really had it.

items.one: Keeping a copy of the answer nearby so you do not have to ask again.
items.like: Writing your best friend's number on your hand instead of looking it up every single time.
items.long: Caches sit everywhere: in your browser, at the CDN, in the app, in front of the database. They make things dramatically faster. The hard part is knowing when the saved answer has gone stale and must be thrown away.
items.why: Most 'why is it showing the old price' bugs are a cache somewhere holding an answer for too long.

groups.title: When lots of people turn up
groups.blurb: Everything works with ten users. This is what changes at ten thousand.

items.one: How wide the pipe is, and how long the journey takes.
items.like: Bandwidth is how many lanes the motorway has. Latency is how far away the city is.
items.long: They are different problems. A very wide pipe to a very distant server is still slow to start. Distance cannot be fixed by paying more, only by putting a copy closer to the person. Light itself takes about 100 milliseconds to go halfway round the world.
items.why: This is the entire reason CDNs exist.

items.one: Copies of your files kept in cities near your visitors.
items.like: A local warehouse in every city, instead of posting everything from one factory.
items.long: CDN means content delivery network. The first person in a city to ask for a file pulls it from your server. Everyone after that gets the nearby copy. It makes things faster and takes load off your server at the same time.
items.why: CloudFront is this. It is usually the cheapest big speed improvement available.

items.one: Something that shares visitors out across several servers.
items.like: The person at the bank who says 'counter three is free'.
items.long: It sits in front and hands each request to whichever server is healthy and least busy. If a server stops answering, it quietly stops sending people there. That is how you reboot a server in the middle of the day without anybody noticing.
items.why: With one server, a reboot is an outage. With a load balancer and two servers, it is nothing.

items.one: Getting a bigger machine, or getting more machines.
items.like: A bigger oven, versus a second oven.
items.long: Up is easy and has a ceiling, because there is a biggest machine and it is very expensive. Out has no real ceiling but your software has to be built for it, and some things, especially databases, are hard to spread across machines.
items.why: Nearly every growth story is: scale up until it hurts, then do the work to scale out.

items.one: How much of the time it is working.
items.like: A shop's opening hours, except everyone expects you to be open all the time.
items.long: 99.9 percent sounds excellent. It is nearly 9 hours of downtime a year. 99.99 percent is under an hour. Each extra nine costs a great deal more than the one before it, so the honest question is what an hour of downtime actually costs you in money.
items.why: People buy expensive redundancy without ever working out what an outage is worth to them.

items.one: A guard deciding what is allowed in and out.
items.like: A doorman with a list. Not on the list, not coming in.
items.long: A security group is a list of rules around one server: which doors are open, and to whom. The sensible default is to deny everything and open only what is genuinely needed. Most breaches are a door someone opened 'just for testing' and forgot.
items.why: A database reachable from the whole internet is the single most common serious mistake in cloud setups.

groups.title: So what is 'the cloud'
groups.blurb: Now this word should finally mean something.

items.one: Renting computers by the hour instead of buying them.
items.like: Taking a taxi rather than buying a car. You pay for the trip. You do not pay for parking, insurance or the mechanic.
items.long: There is no cloud. There are Amazon's buildings, full of Amazon's computers, and you are renting a slice. What changed is not the computers, it is the renting: you can have a server in ninety seconds, and give it back in an hour, and pay for that hour.
items.why: Before this, you bought a server, waited six weeks for delivery, and owned it for five years whether you needed it or not.

items.one: Which city your computers are in, and which building in that city.
items.like: Region is the city. Availability zone is one specific building in it, miles from the others.
items.long: Mumbai is a Region, ap-south-1. Inside it there are several availability zones, separate buildings with separate power and separate connections. Putting your servers in two zones means a fire or a power cut in one building does not stop you.
items.why: Pick the Region closest to your users. Use at least two zones. That one sentence prevents most outages.

items.one: The meter is always running, on everything you left switched on.
items.like: A tap you forgot to turn off. Nobody comes to remind you.
items.long: You are charged for time (a server that is on), storage (per GB per month), requests (per million), and data leaving AWS. That last one catches nearly everybody, because data going in is usually free and data going out is not.
items.why: Set a budget alert on your first day. It has saved more people more money than any other single action.

items.one: Somebody else patches it, backs it up, and gets woken at 3am.
items.like: A serviced flat. You still live there. You do not fix the boiler.
items.long: Running your own database on a server is cheaper on paper. Then you own the patching, the backups, the failover, the monitoring and the 3am phone call. Managed costs more per hour and less per year once you count a person's time.
items.why: For a small team, managed services are almost always the right answer, and the 'saving' from self-hosting is usually imaginary.
